podcast.body: In 1980, a cover version of "Good Vibrations" was used in an advertisement for Sunkist Orange Soda. This commercial passed with "minimal fuss" as it did not feature the original artists' vocals, illustrating a different public perception compared to later instances of direct artist involvement or original song use. "In 1980 when the Beach Boys Good Vibrations was used in an ad for Sunkissed Orn Soda."

podcast.body: Intended as the perfect pop song and the first preview of Smile, its recording incurred a record cost of $50,000, the highest for a single track at the time. It was meticulously recorded in five different studios with up to 26 musicians, involving Wilson creating 28 variations of the verse and 37 of the chorus before selecting the best takes for the final version. The single, released on October 10, 1966, was a huge success, reaching number 1 in both the United States and England, and selling 400,000 copies in just four days. It was described as something "new and exciting," a psychedelic and hip-hop song in equal parts. "Good Vibrations se grabó en cinco estudios diferentes con la participación de hasta 26 músicos, la complejidad del proceso fue inmensa."

podcast.body: This song is noted for its experimental use of a Theremin, an electronic musical instrument that could be played without being touched. The distinctive warbling sound in the track is attributed to this device. "that thing in good vibrations, that's a Theraman."
